reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant disorder caused by variants in LMX1B, a transcription factor for dorsoventral limb patterning
The classic tetrad is dysplastic or absent nails, absent or hypoplastic patellae, elbow abnormalities and iliac horns
Nail changes are usually the earliest and most consistent sign: hypoplastic, ridged, or split nails, often with triangular lunulae, most marked on the thumbs
Absent or small patellae cause recurrent patellar dislocation, knee instability and early degenerative change
Iliac horns, bony spurs projecting posteriorly from the ilia, are pathognomonic and asymptomatic
Elbow involvement includes limited extension, radial head subluxation/dislocation and hypoplastic capitellum
Nephropathy and open-angle glaucoma are important extraskeletal complications that require lifelong monitoring
reference.pathophysiology: Nail-patella syndrome is caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in LMX1B, a LIM-homeodomain transcription factor essential for dorsal patterning of the developing limb and for the differentiation of structures including the glomerular basement membrane and the anterior segment of the eye. Haploinsufficiency disrupts dorsalisation, producing nail hypoplasia, patellar and elbow malformations, and the iliac horns. In the kidney, defective podocyte and basement membrane development can lead to proteinuria and progressive nephropathy, while impaired anterior-segment development predisposes to glaucoma.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated congenital patellar dislocation or aplasia
additionalInvestigations: Skeletal radiographs of pelvis (iliac horns), knees (patellae) and elbows
Urinalysis for proteinuria and monitoring of renal function for nephropathy
Ophthalmological assessment including intraocular pressure for glaucoma
Family assessment given autosomal dominant inheritance
redFlags: Proteinuria or declining renal function heralding progressive nephropathy
Raised intraocular pressure or visual field loss from glaucoma
Recurrent patellar dislocation with disabling knee instability
Signs of nephrotic-range proteinuria requiring nephrology input
reference.prognosis: Most affected individuals have a normal lifespan; morbidity comes from musculoskeletal deformity and, in a subset, from progressive nephropathy that can lead to renal failure, and from glaucoma, both of which are the main determinants of long-term outcome.
pitfalls: Treating it as a purely orthopaedic disorder and failing to monitor for nephropathy and glaucoma
Missing the diagnosis because iliac horns are asymptomatic and not sought on imaging
Overlooking subtle nail changes as the earliest clue
Not screening family members despite clear dominant inheritance
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Manage musculoskeletal manifestations with physiotherapy, bracing and orthopaedic surgery for recurrent patellar dislocation, knee instability and elbow deformity
Monitor renal function with regular urinalysis for proteinuria and treat nephropathy with renin-angiotensin blockade using ACE inhibitors or angiotensin-receptor blockers to reduce proteinuria
Screen for progressive nephropathy and escalate to renal replacement therapy or transplantation in renal failure
Undertake lifelong ophthalmological surveillance for glaucoma with intraocular-pressure monitoring and appropriate glaucoma therapy
Provide analgesia and joint-protection strategies for degenerative joint disease
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal dominant LMX1B disease with molecular confirmation and family assessment
Coordinate multidisciplinary follow-up across orthopaedics, nephrology, ophthalmology and clinical genetics
